props.title: Godard's Passion

sections.content: **Passion** (1982) represents one of Godard's most complex meditations on the relationship between cinema, painting, and labor. The film follows a director struggling to shoot tableaux vivants of classical paintings while a parallel story of factory workers unfolds. Like his earlier **Weekend** (1967) and **Tout va bien** (1972), Godard deliberately disrupts narrative conventions, but here he's specifically interested in how moving images can capture - or fail to capture - the essence of static art. The recreations of works by Rembrandt, Goya, and Delacroix become sites of both visual splendor and ideological tension.

sections.content: Godard's 1980s work marks a distinct shift from his earlier, more politically strident films. While **Passion** (1982) maintains his career-long critique of capitalism and labor relations, it approaches these themes through a more poetic, visually-driven lens. The film shares DNA with **Prénom Carmen** (1983) and **Je vous salue, Marie** (1985) in its investigation of how sacred and profane images collide in modern life. This trilogy represents Godard grappling with questions of beauty and meaning in an increasingly commercialized world.

The film's innovative approach to lighting and composition directly influenced later art-focused cinema like Peter Greenaway's **The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover** (1989) and Derek Jarman's **Caravaggio** (1986). Godard's technique of recreating classical paintings would be echoed in films like **The Mill and the Cross** (2011) and **Shirley: Visions of Reality** (2013), though none match his political urgency. sections.content: Through its parallel storylines of film production and factory labor, **Passion** (1982) interrogates who has the power to look and who is forced to be looked at. This theme connects to earlier New Wave examinations of the male gaze like **2 or 3 Things I Know About Her** (1967) but with a new focus on class relations. The film's factory workers, particularly Isabelle Huppert's character, aren't just objects of the camera's gaze but assert their own right to look and judge.
